description: A HAVING predicate must decide which rows a page contains, not which of an already-chosen page survives. Ordering by name takes a shortcut the other orderings have no equivalent for: it walks the name index in order and stops once it holds LIMIT rows. That is correct while every filter has already run, and wrong once one has not -- HAVING is applied after the page is cut, so the answer becomes the first LIMIT rows by name minus those failing HAVING, instead of the first LIMIT rows by name that satisfy it. Rows that qualify are never fetched, nothing is truncated in the reply, and no error is raised. The pairs below differ in one keyword at a time so the cause cannot be mistaken: WHERE against HAVING at the same limit, and name-ordering against orderings that materialise before paging.

cases.name: the_answer_this_suite_measures_against
cases.description: Ground truth, ordered by a field with no index shortcut so the full candidate set is materialised and HAVING runs before the limit. Seven functions in this corpus exceed 150 lines. Every case below asks for those same seven, or a prefix of them. This case also shares the corpus with the expected failures, so an unregistered corpus cannot pass itself off as the defect.
cases.fql: FIND symbols WHERE fql_kind = 'function' HAVING lines > 150 ORDER BY lines DESC LIMIT 1001

cases.name: a_where_predicate_survives_the_name_ordered_page
cases.description: The control that isolates the keyword. Identical to the case below in every character except WHERE for HAVING. A WHERE predicate filters rows as they are scanned, so the shortcut collects three rows that satisfy it and the answer is right. Keep this passing: if it ever fails, the fault has moved out of HAVING and the case below is no longer measuring what it claims.
cases.fql: FIND symbols WHERE fql_kind = 'function' WHERE lines > 150 ORDER BY name ASC LIMIT 3

cases.name: a_having_predicate_survives_the_name_ordered_page
cases.description: The same three rows, asked for with HAVING instead of WHERE. A page of three is requested and three qualifying rows exist, so three must come back. The shortcut instead takes the first three functions by name -- none of which is long enough -- and applies HAVING to those, returning nothing at all.
cases.expect_fail_reason: ordering by name walks the name index and stops at LIMIT rows before HAVING has run, so the reply is the first LIMIT rows by name minus those failing HAVING rather than the first LIMIT rows by name that satisfy it; the qualifying rows further along the alphabet are never fetched and nothing in the reply says so
cases.fql: FIND symbols WHERE fql_kind = 'function' HAVING lines > 150 ORDER BY name ASC LIMIT 3

cases.name: a_limit_larger_than_the_answer_still_returns_all_of_it
cases.description: A limit far above the seven matching rows cannot bound the answer, so all seven must come back whatever the ordering. Three do: the ones whose names fall inside the window the shortcut stopped at. The other four sort later in the alphabet and are never looked at.
cases.expect_fail_reason: ordering by name walks the name index and stops at LIMIT rows before HAVING has run, so a limit above the size of the answer still truncates it -- the rows that qualify are the ones whose names happen to fall inside the window, not the ones the predicate selects
cases.fql: FIND symbols WHERE fql_kind = 'function' HAVING lines > 150 ORDER BY name ASC LIMIT 1001

cases.name: reversing_the_order_does_not_change_which_rows_qualify
cases.description: The direction of an ORDER BY decides the sequence rows come back in, never which rows are in the answer. Descending must return the same seven as ascending. It returns one -- the single qualifying name that falls inside the window when the walk runs from the other end, which is the clearest statement that the window and not the predicate is choosing the answer.
cases.expect_fail_reason: ordering by name walks the name index and stops at LIMIT rows before HAVING has run, so reversing the direction changes which rows are reachable inside the window and therefore which rows the answer contains
cases.fql: FIND symbols WHERE fql_kind = 'function' HAVING lines > 150 ORDER BY name DESC LIMIT 1001
